items.title: Just-in-time becomes a vulnerability under shock
items.claim: Toyota pioneered just-in-time inventory. What happened to Toyota production during the 2011 Tohoku earthquake?

options.text: Toyota's global production fell by around 800,000 vehicles because a single supplier of microcontrollers (Renesas) was damaged

items.reveal:
Renesas's Naka factory in Ibaraki produced ~30% of automotive microcontrollers globally. After the 11 March 2011 earthquake, Toyota's worldwide output dropped sharply through to mid-2011. After Tohoku, Toyota mandated suppliers to map upstream dependencies and hold buffer stocks for critical components — partially abandoning pure JIT.

The 2020-22 COVID semiconductor shortages repeated the lesson industry-wide.
items.why: Lean optimises against ordinary variation. It does not optimise against catastrophic disruption — and the same firms that pioneered it have had to add 'just-in-case' buffers.

items.title: The Hawthorne effect is real but smaller than the textbook story
items.claim: Elton Mayo's Hawthorne studies (1927-32) are taught as showing that worker productivity rose because of attention paid to them. What does re-analysis of the original data show?

options.text: The effect was even larger than originally reported

Levitt and List's 2011 re-analysis of original records suggests the 'Hawthorne effect' was much weaker than reported; productivity gains were largely explained by which workers were replaced and the Monday rebound after weekends
No data from the studies survived
The lighting reduction was actually the cause

items.reveal:
Steven Levitt and John List (American Economic Journal, 2011) accessed original Hawthorne Works data digitised by the University of Wisconsin. They found the famous 'productivity rose whatever you changed' pattern was much weaker than Mayo claimed and largely artifactual.

The broader 'human relations' school it spawned remained influential — but the founding evidence base was weaker than generations of textbooks suggested.
items.why: Iconic findings get retold long after the evidence has been challenged. Modern HR theory survives, but its founding study should be taught with caveats.

items.title: Demographics often predict less than marketers assume
items.claim: Mark Ritson and others have argued that traditional demographic segmentation (age, income, gender) often performs poorly. What's the evidence?

options.text: Demographics predict purchase behaviour with high accuracy
Within-group variation in purchase behaviour is often larger than between-group variation; behavioural segmentation (what people actually buy) typically outperforms demographic segmentation
Demographics are legally required for marketing
Segmentation has been abandoned in modern marketing

items.reveal:
Byron Sharp's 'How Brands Grow' (2010), drawing on the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, argued that mass-market brands grow through reach, not narrow targeting — and that demographic targeting often misallocates spend. Coca-Cola buyers, Toyota buyers and HSBC customers look broadly similar demographically.

Behavioural segmentation (heavy vs light buyers, lapsed vs active) typically explains more variance. Geographic and psychographic add incremental power.
items.why: Marketing teaching often defaults to demographic segmentation because it's easy to teach and the data is available. The evidence suggests it's a weaker guide than is taught.
